about.title: La Habra Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: La Habra's busiest corridors — La Habra Boulevard, Imperial Highway, Whittier Boulevard, and Lambert Road — see a steady share of the city's reported collisions, with public records showing 206 injury crashes and 303 people hurt in the most recent final reporting year. Fridays between 5 and 7 p.m. tend to bring more reported crashes, likely tied to commuter and weekend traffic converging on these routes. Whatever the cause, the aftermath is often the same: medical appointments, missed work, and calls from an insurance adjuster who doesn't have your interests in mind. LawProactive doesn't practice law; we simply connect La Habra residents who've been injured with an independent personal injury attorney who can evaluate the claim, handle communication with insurers, and help protect evidence before it disappears. There's no cost to get connected, and no obligation to move forward.

whyChoose.title: Why La Habra Residents Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Time Limits Matter
items.desc: California generally allows two years to file a car accident claim, but that window can shrink to as little as six months if a government entity — like the City of La Habra or Orange County — is involved. An attorney can help identify which deadline applies before it passes.

items.title: Fault Doesn't Have to Be All-or-Nothing
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, meaning you may still recover compensation even if you're partly responsible for the crash. An independent attorney can help sort out how fault is allocated and what that means for your claim.

items.title: No Cap on What You Can Pursue for Pain and Suffering
items.desc: Unlike some states, California doesn't limit non-economic damages such as pain and suffering in most car accident cases. This makes it important to have someone document the full impact of your injuries, not just medical bills.

items.question: How long do I have to file a claim after a car accident in La Habra?
items.answer: In most cases, California gives you two years from the date of the crash to file a personal injury lawsuit. If a government entity, such as the City of La Habra, is potentially responsible, that deadline can be as short as six months, so it's best not to wait to have your case reviewed.

items.question: Should I give the other driver's insurance company a recorded statement?
items.answer: Generally, it's wise to avoid giving a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer before speaking with an attorney. Insurance adjusters are trained to ask questions that can be used to reduce or deny your claim. An independent attorney can advise you on what, if anything, to say.

items.question: What if my accident happened at a busy intersection like Imperial Highway or La Habra Boulevard?
items.answer: Crashes on high-traffic corridors like Imperial Highway, La Habra Boulevard, or Lambert Road can involve multiple parties, traffic signal evidence, or nearby surveillance footage. Preserving that evidence quickly matters, since footage and physical evidence can disappear within days. An attorney can help ensure it's collected before it's lost.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge anything to connect me with an attorney?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free service, and attorneys in our network typically work on contingency, meaning there's no fee unless they recover compensation for you.
